blocks.text: 1. Deletion Strategies

blocks.alt: A vector to delete goes through a deletion strategy to be removed from the index

blocks.text: Deletion Strategies closes out the Vector Databases module by covering how vectors get properly removed from the collection.
It covers the final lifecycle operation a stored vector goes through: removal.
2. Why Deletion Isn't Just Skipping A Result
As covered in Document Ingestion, a deleted source document needs its vector actually removed, not just ignored.
Leaving it behind means it could still surface in a future search result.
3. Soft Delete Versus Hard Delete

blocks.alt: Soft delete marks the vector while hard delete removes it

blocks.text: A soft delete marks a vector as removed without physically erasing it; a hard delete removes it entirely.
Those two approaches trade recoverability against storage and correctness guarantees.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Deletion type","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Soft delete","Recoverable, but still consumes storage"],["Hard delete","Storage reclaimed, but not recoverable"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Deletion And Index Structure

blocks.alt: A deleted vector leaves a gap in the index

blocks.text: Just as editing a vector in place is awkward, as covered in Vector Updates, removing an entry can leave gaps in an index's internal structure.
Some indexes handle deletion gracefully; others need periodic cleanup.
5. Cascading Deletes Across Chunks

blocks.alt: A deleted parent document cascades to delete all child chunks

blocks.text: One deleted source document can correspond to many separate chunks, given how chunking splits documents apart.
Every chunk descended from that document needs to be found and removed together.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Deleting only the first chunk of a multi chunk document leaves the remaining chunks searchable and retrievable, meaning the supposedly deleted document can still partially surface in results.

blocks.text: 6. Deletion Propagation Across Replicas

blocks.alt: A primary delete propagates to replica 1 and replica 2

blocks.text: A deletion needs to reach every replica, not just one, the same consistency concern raised for updates.
A lagging replica can briefly still return a document that was already deleted elsewhere.
7. Compliance Driven Deletion

blocks.alt: A user deletion request requires a hard delete

blocks.text: Legal or privacy requirements sometimes demand that deleted data truly be gone, not just hidden.
A soft delete alone may not satisfy that kind of strict, verifiable requirement.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A privacy regulation requiring verifiable data removal requires confirming a hard delete has actually reclaimed the underlying storage, not merely that a soft deleted flag has been set on the record.

blocks.text: 8. Garbage Collection And Reclaimed Space

blocks.alt: Soft-deleted items go through garbage collection to reclaim space

blocks.text: Deleted entries often leave behind unused storage until a dedicated cleanup process reclaims it.
Periodic garbage collection keeps a heavily edited collection efficient, echoing the index health concerns already raised for frequent updates.

blocks.text: 9. Vector Databases: Module Complete
Every topic across this module built toward a complete, durable, and maintainable storage layer.
That closes the Vector Databases module before ANN Search Algorithms begins as the next module.
10. Worked Example
The example below cascades a document deletion across all its associated chunks.

code.content:
vector_store = {
    "doc1_chunk1": {"parent_doc": "doc1", "text": "First part of document one."},
    "doc1_chunk2": {"parent_doc": "doc1", "text": "Second part of document one."},
    "doc2_chunk1": {"parent_doc": "doc2", "text": "Only chunk of document two."},
}

def cascading_delete(vector_store, parent_doc_id):
    # find and remove every chunk belonging to the deleted document
    keys_to_delete = [k for k, v in vector_store.items() if v["parent_doc"] == parent_doc_id]
    for key in keys_to_delete:
        del vector_store[key]
        print(f"  Deleted {key}")
    return keys_to_delete

print(f"Before deletion, total chunks: {len(vector_store)}")
deleted = cascading_delete(vector_store, "doc1")

print(f"\nDeleted {len(deleted)} chunks belonging to doc1")
print(f"Remaining chunks: {list(vector_store.keys())}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows both chunks belonging to doc1 removed together, while doc2's chunk remains untouched, exactly the cascading delete behavior a multi chunk document requires.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Deleting only one chunk of a multi chunk document, leaving the rest still searchable.
Relying on a soft delete alone when a compliance requirement demands verifiable, permanent removal.
Assuming a deletion instantly reaches every replica instead of accounting for propagation delay.
Never running garbage collection on a heavily edited collection, wasting storage over time.

blocks.text: 12. Vector Databases: Module Complete

items: What is a Vector Database introduced the specialized storage layer built for similarity search.
Indexing covered building structures that avoid checking every stored vector per query.
Collections covered grouping related vectors into scoped, logical subsets.
Metadata Filtering covered narrowing results within a collection using structured fields.
Partitioning covered splitting large collections into manageable logical pieces.
Sharding covered spreading data physically across separate machines.
Replication covered keeping identical copies for availability and read scaling.
Compression covered shrinking vector storage without losing too much accuracy.
Persistence covered keeping data durable across restarts and failures.
Vector Updates covered modifying existing vectors as source content changes.
Deletion Strategies closed the module by covering how vectors get properly removed.
Next up: ANN Search Algorithms, covering the specific algorithms behind approximate nearest neighbor search.
